newsitem.title: UK: UK to curb arms sales in human rights drive.
newsitem.headline: UK to curb arms sales in human rights drive.

text.p: Britain, one of the world's leading arms exporters, said on Thursday it would clamp down on sales to certain countries under its commitment to put human rights at the heart of its foreign policy.
The curbs were on a 12-point list of measures unveiled by Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, who said Britain had a duty to demand for others rights it claimed for itself as self-evident.

"These dozen steps will put us at the front of the drive to raise standards of human rights," Cook said in his first major setpiece speech since he took office following Labour's landslide election victory on May 1.
The government is reviewing its criteria for licensing arms sales to give effect to its pledge not to supply equipment that might be used for internal repression.

"The full results of the review will be published shortly, but I can announce today that they will result in changes to the present policy governing the licensing of riot control vehicles, small arms and other equipment for sale to the security forces of certain regimes," Cook said.
He disclosed earlier that Indonesia, accused by human rights groups of using British weapons for internal repression, would be affected by the change in policy.
"There will be changes with respect to a number of countries, of which that is one," he told BBC radio.
Cook later told reporters there was nothing in his speech to undermine Britain's role as a major arms exporter. But he said the government had a responsibility to regulate the arms trade.
"It is in all our interests that we reach an outcome in which we do continue be a leading arms exporter without conflicting with other very important aspects of the British nation," he said.

Cook said some defence firms would be unhappy with the new doctrine, but he recalled that Britain had to write off one billion pounds ($1.67 billion) in export guarantees because weapons sold to Iraqi President Saddam Hussein were not paid for.
"It is perhaps surprising that businesses sometimes require to be reminded that brutal, psychopathic and megalomaniac dictators tend to be rather unreliable paying invoices," he said.
Cook also announced a $1 billion commitment to the Geneva-based International Labour Organisation to help it to tackle the scourge of child labour.

He said Britain would provide 1 million guilders ($495,000) to the International Criminal Tribunal on Yugoslavia, based in The Hague, to build a second courtroom to speed up trials of suspected war criminals by as much as a year.
"It is a practical and effective demonstration of our commitment to upholding international law and bringing justice to those who break it," he said.

Cook reaffirmed that Britain would argue that Nigeria should remain suspended from the Commonwealth, which mainly groups Britain and its former colonies, unless the government's performance on human rights improved radically.
But he said it would be a mistake simply to sever links with every country that had an unsatisfactory rights record.
"This may provide us with clean hands, but it is unlikely to provide their people with better rights," he said.
"Some regimes, such as Iraq, may simply be beyond rational persuasion, but wherever possible our approach should be to encourage improved standards through dialogue."
